title: A Brutal King and His End
overview: Jehoram, king of Judah, murders his brothers and turns the nation to other gods, and the chapter traces the losses, warning and painful death that the writer presents as God's judgment on him.

parts.label: A murderous start (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons wealth and fortified towns but the throne to his eldest, Jehoram, who once secure killed all his brothers and some of the nation's officials. His marriage to a daughter of Ahab, the northern king known for promoting other gods, shaped his rule, yet God's promise to keep a 'lamp' (a living heir) for David's family kept the royal line from being wiped out.

parts.label: Edom and Libnah break away (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Edom, a neighboring nation to the southeast that had been under Judah's control, rebelled, and Jehoram only escaped by breaking out of an encirclement at night. Libnah, a town within Judah, also revolted, and the writer ties this to Jehoram building hilltop shrines and leading the people to other gods, pictured as unfaithfulness in a marriage.

parts.label: A letter from Elijah (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: The prophet Elijah sends a written message naming Jehoram's crimes and warning of disaster on his household and a slow, terrible illness of the bowels. The books of Kings seem to place Elijah's departure earlier, so scholars are unsure whether he wrote it in advance, whether the dates overlap, or whether the name was later confused with his successor Elisha.

parts.label: Raids on the palace (vv. 16-17)
parts.note: Philistines and Arab groups from the south invade, loot the royal palace and carry off Jehoram's wives and sons. Only his youngest son is left; the Hebrew here calls him Jehoahaz, which uses the same two name parts as Ahaziah in reverse order.

parts.label: A painful, unmourned death (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: After two years of illness Jehoram dies in agony, and the people do not light the honorary fire, probably of spices, that earlier kings received. He is buried in Jerusalem but kept out of the royal tombs, and the text says flatly that no one regretted his passing.

disagreement: Christians differ on how directly to read the raids and illness as God personally punishing Jehoram, with some taking it as straightforward cause and effect and others seeing it as the writer's way of interpreting history to show that rulers answer for how they use power.
think: The people let Jehoram's death pass without honor. What do you think the way a community responds to someone's death can reveal about how that person used their power?
